title: 09. Storage, CDN & Data Engineering: File Storage

objectives: What are POSIX semantics, and why do they matter for file storage but not for object storage?
What is the difference between NFS and SMB, and when would you choose each?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** File storage is a hierarchical storage service that presents data as files and directories in a tree, accessed by multiple clients over standard network protocols (NFS, SMB) with POSIX semantics — providing shared access, file locking, and a familiar filesystem API that legacy applications can mount without modification.

File storage is the storage layer that pretends to be a USB drive shared across the network. When you mount an NFS share on a Linux box or map an SMB share on Windows, you get a directory tree that looks and behaves exactly like a local filesystem: you `cd` into folders, `ls` to list files, `open()` to read or write, and `flock()` to coordinate concurrent access. The catch is that the bytes live on a remote appliance — a NAS (Network Attached Storage) filer in the enterprise data center, or a managed service like AWS EFS, Azure Files, or Google Cloud Filestore in the cloud — and every operation becomes a network RPC. The familiar POSIX semantics (hierarchical namespace, file locking, permissions, append, random read/write) are preserved by the protocol, but at the cost of 1–5ms of network overhead per operation, which is why file storage sits between block storage (sub-ms, single-attach) and object storage (20–50ms, REST) in the latency hierarchy.

The architecture of a file storage system is a cluster of filer nodes that jointly present a single namespace to clients. Each filer runs a metadata service that tracks the directory tree (inodes, directory entries, permissions) and a data service that stores the actual file contents. On AWS EFS, the metadata and data are separated: a metadata service tracks each file's inode and which data chunks hold its contents, while a data service stores chunks erasure-coded across many storage nodes. Files are striped across multiple data nodes for throughput, and the metadata service is replicated for availability. The access protocol is NFSv4 (or SMB for Windows), which is a stateful protocol: a client opens a file, gets a file handle, and the filer tracks the open file and any byte-range locks. This statefulness is what enables the "shared access with locking" use case that object storage cannot serve — multiple clients can mount the same filesystem, and POSIX locking ensures that two writers do not corrupt each other's edits. EFS scales to petabytes and tens of thousands of concurrent mounts with no provisioning — you pay for what you store ($0.30/GB-month Standard, much higher than S3) and the throughput scales with capacity (50 KB/s per GB stored, with burst credit for spiky workloads).

The defining trade-off of file storage is shareability-over-cost. A single EFS filesystem can be mounted by thousands of EC2 instances across all AZs in a region simultaneously, all reading and writing the same files — something that block storage cannot do (single-attach by default) and object storage cannot do well (no append, no locking, no POSIX semantics). This makes file storage the right choice for: shared application configuration (many web servers reading the same config directory), content management systems (WordPress media uploads shared across multiple frontends), ML training scripts and datasets mounted on a GPU cluster, dev/test home directories shared across jump hosts, and lift-and-shift migrations of on-prem applications that expect an NFS mount. The cost is significant: EFS Standard at $0.30/GB-month is ~13x the cost of S3 Standard and ~3x the cost of EBS gp3, and Infrequent Access tier at $0.025/GB-month is still slightly more than S3 Standard. For workloads that do not need shared access, file storage is the wrong choice.

The real-world example that crystallizes the trade-off is Netflix's shared configuration directory. Netflix's hundreds of microservices share a common set of configuration files — Cassandra cluster topology, security credentials, deployment manifests — that must be readable by every service instance and occasionally writable by a config management service. In the early days this was a single NFS mount on every EC2 instance, served by a NetApp filer; as Netflix grew to thousands of instances, the NFS filer became a bottleneck and they migrated to EFS, which scales horizontally and supports 25,000+ concurrent mounts per filesystem. The key advantage over S3: the services can use `flock()` to coordinate config updates, can `inotify`-watch for changes, and can read the files with standard `open()/read()` syscalls without HTTP overhead — important because some legacy libraries had no S3 client. The key advantage over EBS: one EFS filesystem serves every instance across all AZs, so a failed AZ does not break config access for survivors. The cost — about $0.30/GB-month for a few hundred GB of config — is negligible compared to the operational benefit, but the same pattern at petabyte scale would be prohibitively expensive and would move to S3 with a sync agent.

Another canonical example is the ML training workload: a team of data scientists runs GPU training jobs on a Kubernetes cluster, and the training scripts, hyperparameter configs, and small datasets need to be available on every GPU node. Mounting an EFS filesystem at `/mnt/shared` on every pod gives every job instant access to the same files, with standard POSIX semantics for reading and writing checkpoints. For large datasets (terabytes of training data), EFS is too expensive — the pattern there is to use S3 as the source of truth, and either sync to local NVMe (instance store) at job start or use a tool like JuiceFS that presents S3 as a POSIX filesystem with local caching. The architectural lesson is: file storage for shared small files that need POSIX semantics and frequent access; object storage for large immutable blobs; block storage for single-instance random I/O.

The cost model has gotten more nuanced with the introduction of EFS IA (Infrequent Access) and Intelligent Tiering. A workload that has a hot working set of 100GB accessed daily and a cold archive of 1TB accessed monthly can use lifecycle policies to age cold files to IA, paying $0.025/GB-month for the cold 1TB (=$25/month) and $0.30/GB-month for the hot 100GB (=$30/month) — total $55/month, versus $330/month if everything were in Standard. The throughput-per-GB model also matters: a small EFS filesystem (100GB) gets only 5 MB/s throughput baseline, which is insufficient for many workloads — you either provision more storage (and pay for capacity you don't need) or use the Infrequent Access tier to absorb cold data and free up the Standard tier's throughput for hot data. For high-throughput shared storage, the alternative is FSx for Lustre (AWS's managed Lustre), which provides hundreds of GB/s of throughput for HPC workloads at a higher price — designed specifically for ML and HPC, not for general-purpose file sharing.

### Mermaid Diagram ```mermaid flowchart TD C1[Client 1
EC2 mount] -->|NFSv4 RPC| GW[Protocol Gateway] C2[Client 2
EC2 mount] -->|NFSv4 RPC| GW C3[Client 3
on-prem] -->|SMB RPC| GW GW --> MD[(Metadata Service
inodes, dir tree, locks)] GW --> DS[(Data Service
erasure-coded chunks)] MD <--> DS DS --> N1[Storage Node 1] DS --> N2[Storage Node 2] DS --> N3[Storage Node 3] IA[Cold files] -.->|lifecycle age| IAS[(Infrequent Access tier)] ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` Client A (mount /mnt/shared) --+ Client B (mount /mnt/shared) --+--> NFSv4 RPC --> Protocol GW Client C (Windows, SMB) --+ | v +--------------------------+ | Metadata Service | | inode table | | dir tree: /a/b/c.txt | | locks: file=X, range=.. | +--------------------------+ | v +--------------------------+ | Data Service (chunks) | | file id=42 -> [c1,c2,c3] | | erasure coded across | | storage nodes | +--------------------------+ | lifecycle: cold -> IA tier ``` ### Walkthrough 1. A client mounts the filesystem via NFSv4 (or SMB), establishing a stateful session with the protocol gateway; subsequent file operations use file handles that the metadata service tracks. 2. A `read()` syscall on a path resolves the directory tree through the metadata service to an inode and a list of chunk IDs, which the data service fetches from storage nodes and returns to the client. 3. Concurrent writes to the same file coordinate via byte-range locks held in the metadata service, ensuring POSIX semantics; cold files age to the IA tier via lifecycle policy to reduce cost.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
"""
Mini file storage mock: hierarchical directory tree, POSIX-ish file ops,
byte-range locking for concurrent writers, and an NFS-style 'mount' that
many clients can share. Demonstrates the metadata/data separation.
"""
import time, uuid
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class Inode:
    inode_id: str
    is_dir: bool
    size: int = 0
    blocks: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)   # chunk IDs in data svc
    children: dict[str, "Inode"] = field(default_factory=dict)
    locks: dict = field(default_factory=dict)   # range -> client_id
    mtime: float = time.time()

class FileStorage:
    """NFS-like shared filesystem: one namespace, many clients."""
    def __init__(self):
        self.root = Inode(inode_id="root", is_dir=True)
        self._data_chunks: dict[str, bytes] = {}     # data service
        self._lock_holders: dict[str, str] = {}      # file_id -> client_id

    def _resolve(self, path: str, create_dirs: bool = False) -> Inode:
        parts = [p for p in path.strip("/").split("/") if p]
        node = self.root
        for i, p in enumerate(parts):
            if not node.is_dir:
                raise NotADirectoryError(path)
            if p not in node.children:
                if create_dirs and i == len(parts) - 1:
                    new = Inode(inode_id=str(uuid.uuid4()),
                                is_dir=False if i == len(parts) - 1 else True)
                    node.children[p] = new
                    node = new
                    continue
                raise FileNotFoundError(path)
            node = node.children[p]
        return node

    def mkdir(self, path: str):
        parent_path, _, name = path.rpartition("/")
        parent = self._resolve("/" + parent_path) if parent_path else self.root
        if name in parent.children:
            raise FileExistsError(path)
        parent.children[name] = Inode(inode_id=str(uuid.uuid4()), is_dir=True)

    def write(self, path: str, data: bytes, client_id: str):
        node = self._resolve(path, create_dirs=True)
        chunk_id = str(uuid.uuid4())
        self._data_chunks[chunk_id] = data     # write to data service
        node.blocks = [chunk_id]               # overwrite = new chunk
        node.size = len(data)
        node.mtime = time.time()

    def read(self, path: str) -> bytes:
        node = self._resolve(path)
        if node.is_dir:
            raise IsADirectoryError(path)
        return b"".join(self._data_chunks[c] for c in node.blocks)

    def list_dir(self, path: str = "/") -> list[str]:
        node = self._resolve(path)
        if not node.is_dir:
            raise NotADirectoryError(path)
        return sorted(node.children.keys())

    def lock_file(self, path: str, client_id: str) -> bool:
        """Advisory lock, like NFS flock(): one writer at a time."""
        node = self._resolve(path)
        if node.inode_id in self._lock_holders:
            return self._lock_holders[node.inode_id] == client_id
        self._lock_holders[node.inode_id] = client_id
        return True

    def unlock_file(self, path: str, client_id: str):
        node = self._resolve(path)
        if self._lock_holders.get(node.inode_id) == client_id:
            del self._lock_holders[node.inode_id]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    fs = FileStorage()
    fs.mkdir("/apps")
    fs.mkdir("/apps/web")

    # Two clients mount the same namespace
    fs.write("/apps/web/config.yaml", b"name: prod\nreplicas: 3\n",
             client_id="web-1")
    print("web-1 reads:", fs.read("/apps/web/config.yaml").decode())

    print("Listing /apps/web:", fs.list_dir("/apps/web"))

    # Concurrent write coordination
    print("web-1 lock:", fs.lock_file("/apps/web/config.yaml", "web-1"))
    print("web-2 lock (blocked):", fs.lock_file("/apps/web/config.yaml", "web-2"))
    fs.unlock_file("/apps/web/config.yaml", "web-1")
    print("web-2 lock (after release):",
          fs.lock_file("/apps/web/config.yaml", "web-2"))
```

quiz.question: What are POSIX semantics, and why do they matter for file storage but not for object storage?
options: EFS's throughput is proportional to the amount of Standard-tier storage you have: 50 KB/s per GB stored, with a burst credit system that allows up to 100 MB/s for short periods.
FSx for Lustre is a managed Lustre filesystem — Linux-only, HPC-optimized, hundreds of GB/s throughput, sub-ms latency, integrates with S3 (can read S3 objects as files natively),…
The performance difference is small (both are 1–5ms per operation), and the protocol choice is rarely the bottleneck.
These semantics matter because legacy applications — databases, content management systems, build tools, dev environments — were written assuming a POSIX filesystem and break if those…
quiz.explanation: POSIX (Portable Operating System Interface) semantics define the behavior of a Unix-compatible filesystem: a hierarchical directory tree, atomic rename, byte-range locking (flock/fcntl), permissions (uid/gid/mode), append, random read/write at any offset, and fsync() for durability.

quiz.question: What is the difference between NFS and SMB, and when would you choose each?
options: These semantics matter because legacy applications — databases, content management systems, build tools, dev environments — were written assuming a POSIX filesystem and break if those…

FSx for Lustre is a managed Lustre filesystem — Linux-only, HPC-optimized, hundreds of GB/s throughput, sub-ms latency, integrates with S3 (can read S3 objects as files natively),…
The performance difference is small (both are 1–5ms per operation), and the protocol choice is rarely the bottleneck.
quiz.explanation: NFS (Network File System) is the Unix-native protocol, originally from Sun in 1984, now at version 4.1 / 4.2. It uses stateful connections (NFSv4), supports POSIX semantics natively (file locking, async writes, delegations), and is the default for Linux workloads. SMB (Server Message Block), also known as CIFS, is the Windows-native protocol, originally from IBM in 1983, now at version 3.1.1.

quiz.question: How does file storage handle concurrent writes from multiple clients, and what are the failure modes?
options: The problem is that media uploads are local to each server, so user A's upload to server 1 is invisible to user B's request routed to server 2.
S3 is fundamentally an object store, not a POSIX filesystem, and Hadoop/Spark were originally designed for HDFS's POSIX-like semantics.
Enable EFS Intelligent Tiering with a lifecycle policy that moves files not accessed in 30 days to the Infrequent Access (IA) tier.
File storage uses byte-range locks (flock for whole-file, fcntl for byte ranges) coordinated through the metadata service.
quiz.explanation: File storage uses byte-range locks (flock for whole-file, fcntl for byte ranges) coordinated through the metadata service. When client A calls flock(file, LOCK_EX), the metadata service records A as the lock holder; if client B then calls flock on the same file, it blocks until A releases the lock or the lease expires.

quiz.explanation: EFS's throughput is proportional to the amount of Standard-tier storage you have: 50 KB/s per GB stored, with a burst credit system that allows up to 100 MB/s for short periods. A 100GB filesystem therefore has a baseline of 5 MB/s and can burst to 100 MB/s until the burst credit (also proportional to size) is exhausted — after which it drops to 5 MB/s, often causing application timeouts.

quiz.question: How does file storage compare to object storage for a data lake, and when does each win?
options: The right choice is EFS, with the cache structured to maximize read amplification.
EFS supports encryption at rest with AWS KMS customer-managed CMKs.
Use AWS FSx for Windows File Server, which is a managed SMB filesystem with full Active Directory integration.
Object storage wins for data lake "data at rest" — S3's $0.023/GB-month, 11-nines durability, and decoupling of storage from compute make it the default for…
quiz.explanation: Object storage wins for data lake "data at rest" — S3's $0.023/GB-month, 11-nines durability, and decoupling of storage from compute make it the default for petabyte-scale analytics (Snowflake, Athena, Databricks all read from S3).
